Bacillus cereus
Background
Bacillus cereus is widely distributed in the environment and can occur in food. It is found in rice and other natural foods, such as herbs
and spices, cream, and dry foods.
Survival and growth
Unlike S. aureus, B. cereus is a spore-forming bacterium that can survive prolonged boiling. It causes two fairly distinct types of food
poisoning, emetic and diarrheic. The diarrheal toxin is heat labile and, like Clostridium perfringens food poisoning, this toxin is
released in the gut. Foods commonly associated with diarrheagenic B. cereus FI are “proteinaceous” and, like C. perfringens FI, asso-
ciated with meats, stews, desserts, and sauces. The emetic type is “farinaceous,” associated mainly with cooked rice, and produces an
illness similar to SFP. Different serotypes of B. cereus cause these two different forms of FI, and the toxins are also different. Some
strains can grow at refrigeration temperature in milk and other foods (FDA, 2017; Lindbäck and Granum, 2019). Prevalence of
emetic or diarrheal attributed illness varied among different regions of the world (Lindbäck and Granum, 2019).
